prize_parts.citation: For a visionary, densely patterned prose, rooted in his poetry, that joins memory, the body and metaphysical dream into a singular imaginative architecture.

statement.case_for: My configuration is unchanged, but the grounds are narrower and I hold them with more caution than in round 1. The criterion I started from is a voice found in this writer's work and nowhere else. On public knowledge, Cărtărescu meets it in the long, rhythmically built sentences of the Blinding trilogy and in Solenoid, where memory, the body, Bucharest and metaphysical speculation form one construction. In answer to the chair's question about variation versus recurrence, I can only offer what general public knowledge suggests, and I have not verified it. Solenoid seems to work in a different register from the trilogy: a more diaristic, first-person, everyday frame from which the visionary material rises, and not a second performance of the same architecture. If that holds, recurring images (the body, the city, the dream) are structural motifs within a developing project. If a reader of the Romanian original finds that the late volumes only re-stage earlier material, the case weakens. I would accept a citation limited to prose with the poetry named only as a root. That is where the evidence is strongest, and it avoids claiming a whole-oeuvre breadth I cannot assess. The case rests on the construction and language of the books. It does not rest on post-communist context, reputation, or the fact that several colleagues rank him highly, which is not evidence of merit.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation remains the length and possible self-recurrence of the late novels, as Olsson says. A second is that the effect depends on Romanian syntax and rhythm that I can judge only through translation. A third is that the poetry and early prose are unevenly covered in translation, so a citation naming poetry rests on thinner evidence than one naming the novels. If the committee cannot establish development in the later books, Can Xue's compression or Carson's formal economy could reasonably outweigh scale under the criterion of sustained quality. I cannot dismiss that. The weighting of architectural scale against compact formal range is a real difference of judgment, and I do not claim it is settled by anything in the record.

responses.point: Olsson ranks Can Xue first for a sustained, uncompromising anti-realist voice. He holds that the major Cărtărescu novels are long and sometimes repetitive, and he weighs formal economy more heavily. He asks what evidence would move members on B003.
responses.response: I take the economy point seriously. It is the main risk to my choice, and I do not treat the Cărtărescu case as closed. On Can Xue, what would move me toward B003 is evidence from a reader of the Chinese originals that the later books change the terms of her method, whether in scale, in the relation of short fiction to the novel, or in the sentences themselves, and that the strangeness is built into the language and not supplied by interpretive projection. Without that, I cannot tell depth from consistency, and for me the question is as open for her as the repetition question is for Cărtărescu. I keep her as my first alternative. In a fallback she would come before Carson because her formal break is more radical and compressed, and I see that as a judgment about weighting, not a difference I can demonstrate.

responses.point: Carlberg ranks Carson first. She would write the citation on the original poetry, essays and verse-novel forms, treat translations as context, and argues that recurring concerns (desire, loss, the classical text, the fragment) form a method and not one-off experiments.
responses.response: Her answer on scope helps. A citation resting on poetry, essay and hybrid narrative and leaving translation out as a ground meets most of my round-1 objection, so I now regard Carson as a stronger alternative than my fifth place implied. Two doubts remain. The durable-core claim is made from general knowledge of the main volumes, and Carlberg says herself that she has not verified the later ones. And some of the effects, above all in Nox, depend on material form that I cannot judge from the text. I would want the committee to test the core against the whole bibliography. I do not read her honest narrowing of the margin as an argument for or against anyone.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg shares my first choice but would keep the citation tied to the large-scale prose, with poetry secondary. He separates repetition of motif from repetition of method and rests his case on development and scale.
responses.response: I agree with his distinction between recurring motif and recurring method, and it is the test I would apply to the late novels. I also accept his narrower citation. Having him and Sward agree with me is not corroboration, since we share the same limits: translation and uneven coverage of the poetry. I therefore propose to name the poetry only as the root of the prose, and to drop even that if the committee's readers find nothing in it that supports the claim.

responses.point: Palm ranks Carson first. She weighs line-level control and formal economy above scale and names the hardest question as whether the hybrid forms are a sustained achievement or a narrowly appealing erudite mode.
responses.response: That weighting is the actual divide between us, and I think the chair is right that it, and not translation, now separates B045 from B004. I give more weight to sustained construction across large forms. Palm gives more to economy at the level of the line. Both are defensible readings of the common criteria. Her point that Autobiography of Red works as a text without its design carries weight with me. I cannot settle whether the hybrid practice is a lasting body of work or a mode, and I would not claim to.

uncertainties: Translation: I cannot assess the effect of Cărtărescu's dense Romanian prose in translation, and the same limit applies to Can Xue and to Carson's non-English reception.
Corpus coverage: the poetry, essays and early prose are unevenly translated, so any citation clause beyond the major prose rests on partial public knowledge.
Whether the late long novels vary or recur is still unresolved. My view that Solenoid works in a different register from the trilogy comes from general public knowledge and is unverified.
Whether Can Xue's method develops, and whether her strangeness is built into the sentences, cannot be settled without readers of the Chinese originals or regional expert reports.
Whether Carson's durable core is sufficient and how translations and book-design effects count affects how far she can be compared on equal terms.
I have not independently verified any text or source and rely on the supplied entries and general public knowledge.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. My documented connections are to committee colleagues and to the Gothenburg and West Sweden press, and none concerns a shortlisted writer. My own practice as a historical novelist is context only and is not evidence of preference.
